title: Troubleshooting network connectivity
learningObjective: Find why two Azure resources can't connect, using effective routes, effective security rules and Network Watcher tools.
foundation: When a connection fails, check each hop in order: source NSG outbound, routing, destination NSG inbound, then the guest OS firewall and the application.
Network Watcher is Azure's built-in toolkit for this. It's enabled automatically per region.
engineer: IP flow verify: tests one 5-tuple against the VM's NSGs (subnet and network card, NIC). Answers Allow or Deny, and names the rule.
NSG diagnostics: like IP flow verify, but shows the result at the subnet level and the network card level separately.
Next hop: for a destination, shows where a VM sends the traffic: the next hop type, its IP, and which route table decided.
Effective security rules and effective routes (on the network card): what Azure really applies, with everything merged.

Connection troubleshoot: a real TCP or ICMP test from a VM (or Bastion, or Application Gateway) to a destination. It shows each hop, the delay, and what failed, including when the destination simply doesn't answer (for example a stopped service).
Packet capture: records the traffic on a VM.
VNet flow logs: record IP flows for later analysis. NSG flow logs are being retired: you can't create new ones after 30 June 2025.
Agent needed: Connection troubleshoot and packet capture need the Network Watcher agent extension on the VM.
Check in this order: NSG outbound; route; NSG inbound; the OS firewall; the app.

animation.caption: Troubleshoot connectivity tab: pick a tool and see whether it reveals the hidden fault.

example.title: An app can't reach its database
body: IP flow verify says Allow. Next hop says VnetLocal, so routing is fine. Connection troubleshoot says the destination port isn't reachable. The cause: the SQL Server service had stopped after patching.

prerequisites: An Azure subscription and a resource group (rg-net)
permissions: Network Contributor, or a custom role with Network Watcher permissions plus read access to the VMs
limits: See Azure networking limits in the subscription service limits page
portal: Network Watcher > IP flow verify: choose VM, NIC, protocol, direction, local/remote IP and port.
Network Watcher > Next hop: VM, source IP, destination IP.
Network Watcher > Connection troubleshoot: source VM, destination and port.
VM > Networking > Effective security rules; NIC > Effective routes.
configuration.cli:
az network watcher test-ip-flow -g rg-net --vm web-vm --direction Outbound --protocol TCP --local 10.1.1.4:60000 --remote 10.1.2.4:1433
az network watcher show-next-hop -g rg-net --vm web-vm --source-ip 10.1.1.4 --dest-ip 10.1.2.4
az network watcher test-connectivity -g rg-net --source-resource web-vm --dest-address 10.1.2.4 --dest-port 1433
az network nic list-effective-nsg -g rg-net -n web-vm-nic
configuration.powershell:
$nw = Get-AzNetworkWatcher -Location eastus
$vm = Get-AzVM -Name web-vm -ResourceGroupName rg-net
Test-AzNetworkWatcherIPFlow -NetworkWatcher $nw -TargetVirtualMachineId $vm.Id -Direction Outbound -Protocol TCP -LocalIPAddress 10.1.1.4 -LocalPort 60000 -RemoteIPAddress 10.1.2.4 -RemotePort 1433
Get-AzNetworkWatcherNextHop -NetworkWatcher $nw -TargetVirtualMachineId $vm.Id -SourceIPAddress 10.1.1.4 -DestinationIPAddress 10.1.2.4
Test-AzNetworkWatcherConnectivity -NetworkWatcher $nw -SourceId $vm.Id -DestinationAddress 10.1.2.4 -DestinationPort 1433

lab.objective: Match each fault to the Network Watcher tool that reveals it.
steps: Run the default (Next hop against an NSG fault) and read why it can't see it.
Set fault to 'SQL service stopped' and find the only tool that detects it.
expected: NSG faults: IP flow verify / effective rules

validation.text: Found a root cause with the right tool

failureScenarios: Using Next hop for NSG problems
lab.cost: None. The simulation runs entirely in the browser.

troubleshooting.symptom: IP flow verify says Allow, but the connection fails.
troubleshooting.cause: The problem is routing, the OS firewall or the app.
troubleshooting.fix: Use Next hop and Connection troubleshoot.

troubleshooting.cause: The Network Watcher agent extension is missing.
troubleshooting.fix: Install the extension (Azure installs it automatically when it can).

comparisons.service: AWS Reachability Analyzer and VPC Flow Logs
comparisons.difference: AWS's tools for path checks and flow logs.
Tests from inside the VM, but doesn't tell you which Azure rule blocks the traffic.

misconceptions.myth: If NSGs allow it, the app must be reachable.
misconceptions.reality: No. Routes, the OS firewall and the app itself can still block it.

misconceptions.myth: You have to buy Network Watcher separately.
misconceptions.reality: No. It's turned on automatically. Some features (flow logs, Connection Monitor) cost money.

architectureDecisions: Check one hop at a time: NSG out, route, NSG in, OS, app.
Turn on VNet flow logs early: on important networks, before anything goes wrong.

walkthrough.subtitle: Find out why two things cannot talk, step by step, with Network Watcher.
learn: A checklist from source to destination
IP flow verify and effective security rules
Connection troubleshoot, packet capture and flow logs

steps.label: Can't connect
steps.title: 'The app server cannot reach the database'
body: That sentence could mean a stopped VM, a blocking NSG, a wrong route, a DNS error or a firewall inside the OS. Guessing wastes hours.

steps.label: Checklist
steps.title: Walk the path
body: Check in order: is the VM running? Does DNS resolve? Does the source NSG allow outbound? Which route is used? Does the destination NSG allow inbound? Is the app listening, and is the OS firewall open?

steps.label: NSG tools
steps.title: Is a security rule blocking it?
body: IP flow verify tests one packet (direction, protocol, ports, IPs) and names the rule that allows or denies it. Effective security rules shows the combined rules of the NIC and subnet NSGs.

steps.label: Route tools
steps.title: Is traffic going the right way?
body: Next hop shows where a packet would go and which route table decided it. Effective routes on a NIC lists every route in force.

steps.label: Deeper
steps.title: When you need more
body: Connection troubleshoot tests a real connection end to end and reports where it fails. Packet capture records traffic on a VM. VNet flow logs record allowed and denied flows for later analysis (they replace NSG flow logs). Connection monitor watches a path continuously.

callout.text: Network Watcher is enabled automatically per region when you create a VNet.

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: Troubleshooting
body: Walk the path; let the tools name the culprit.
recap: Running? DNS? NSG out? Route? NSG in? App listening?
IP flow verify names the blocking rule
Effective security rules = NIC + subnet NSGs
Next hop / effective routes for routing
Connection troubleshoot, packet capture, VNet flow logs

handsOn.title: Diagnose a blocked port with Network Watcher
handsOn.cost: Low. One B1s VM costs about US$0.01 per hour. Delete the same day.
before: Signed in at portal.azure.com as Owner of a subscription (a free or pay-as-you-go account works). Work in a resource group called rg-az104-lab.
If rg-az104-lab does not exist yet: search 'Resource groups' > Create > name rg-az104-lab, region UAE North (or any region near you) > Review + create > Create.

A virtual network vnet-lab (10.10.0.0/16) in rg-az104-lab with a subnet snet-app (10.10.1.0/24): Virtual networks > + Create > IP addresses tab. For these labs, untick 'Enable private subnet' on snet-app so lab VMs can reach the internet (in production use a NAT gateway instead).

A small Linux VM vm-lab in snet-app of vnet-lab: Virtual machines > + Create. Image Ubuntu 24.04, size Standard_B1s, password authentication, Networking tab: vnet-lab / snet-app, public IP: None, NIC network security group: Basic, public inbound ports: None. If the VM cannot reach the internet later, its subnet is private (the default for new networks): open the virtual network > Subnets, untick 'Enable private subnet', save, then stop and start the VM. In production use a NAT gateway instead.

steps.do: Search 'Network Watcher' > Network diagnostic tools > IP flow verify. VM: vm-lab, protocol TCP, direction Inbound, local port 22, remote IP 203.0.113.10, remote port 50000. Check.
steps.see: Access denied, with the rule DenyAllInBound named.

steps.do: Open vm-lab > Networking > Network settings > Create port rule > Inbound port rule. Source: IP addresses 203.0.113.10, destination port 22, TCP, Allow, priority 300, name allow-ssh-test. Add.
Run IP flow verify again with the same values.
Open Network Watcher > Effective security rules, choose vm-lab's NIC.
steps.see: All rules in force, including the default rules at priorities 65000–65500.

steps.do: Open Network Watcher > Connection troubleshoot. Source: vm-lab, destination URI www.microsoft.com, port 443. Run.
steps.see: Either Reachable, or Unreachable with the hop where it failed (private subnets without NAT have no internet).

steps.do: Open Network Watcher > Topology (or the VNet > Diagram) for vnet-lab.
steps.see: A picture of the VNet, subnets, NIC and NSG.

check: IP flow verify showed denied, then allowed, naming the rule each time.
cleanup: When you finish for the day: Resource groups > rg-az104-lab > Delete resource group > type the name > Delete. This removes everything inside it.
